title: Nonholonomic Motion Planning
notes: Open by separating ordinary obstacle-avoidance planning from planning under velocity constraints. In this chapter the planner cannot draw an arbitrary curve in configuration space and then ask the robot to follow it. The constructive question is sharper: given a bracket-generating distribution, what input history actually realizes the hidden displacement? Point to the source span and notebook path as the grounded reading route.

title: Three Planning Strategies
notes: Use the three columns as a taxonomy of methods, not as mutually exclusive camps. Optimal control gives principled costs but can be hard to solve. Piecewise-constant words expose Lie brackets and are especially clean for nilpotent systems. Canonical paths package known maneuvers into reusable primitives. The rest of the lecture moves among these strategies as the system class changes.

title: Brockett System As The First Test Case
notes: Brockett's three-state system is the smallest serious demonstration of constructive nonholonomy. The first two states follow the inputs directly, but the third state records the signed area swept by those direct coordinates. Ask students to inspect the figure as a control-space loop: returning to the origin in q1 and q2 is compatible with a nonzero endpoint in q3.

title: Why The Optimal Input Is A Sinusoid
notes: The variational calculation should be read as a geometry generator. The multiplier for the bracket constraint is constant, so the input derivative is obtained by multiplying by a fixed skew matrix. A fixed skew matrix rotates vectors without changing their norm, which is why the optimal input is sinusoidal. The frequency is then selected by the endpoint closure condition.

title: First-Order Canonical Systems
notes: Move from the three-state example to the m-input canonical system by naming the state split. The q_i coordinates are directly actuated, while the q_ij coordinates are first bracket coordinates. The steering algorithm is deliberately staged: first place the directly controlled coordinates, then use closed sinusoidal loops to write the desired skew matrix without disturbing the direct coordinates.

title: Second-Order Bracket Directions
notes: This slide explains why the first-order recipe does not simply scale up. At second order, Jacobi relations and bracket nesting matter, and optimal inputs can leave the elementary sinusoid class. The constructive workaround is staged rectification: steer direct coordinates, correct first brackets, then choose frequencies whose products leave a zero-frequency term only in the desired second-order coordinate.

title: One-Chain Systems
notes: Present the one-chain form as the chapter's clean higher-order model. The vector field g1 shifts information down the chain while g2 injects the second coordinate. Repeated brackets ad_g1^k g2 pick off successive coordinates, so the proof of controllability is nearly a basis count. The diagram is meant to make that bracket ladder visible.

title: Chained-Form Harmonics
notes: The harmonic artifact is the operational memory for Algorithm 3. The input u1 oscillates at the base frequency while u2 is chosen at the kth harmonic. As products are integrated down the chain, all nonmatching harmonics average away and a constant term remains in q_{k+2}. That is why the endpoint formula contains a factorial and powers of the amplitude.

title: Fourier Corrections In Real Systems
notes: Emphasize that real models rarely arrive already in chained form. The chapter's hopping-robot and car examples use coordinate changes and then treat nonlinear leftovers by Fourier coefficients. The pedagogical point is not that nonlinear terms vanish, but that the target displacement can be tied to a specific harmonic coefficient. Students should see the Fourier coefficient as a correction, not a decorative analysis step.

title: Conversion To Chained Form
notes: This is the coordinate-hygiene slide. A nonlinear system can be steered with chained-form tools only after a legitimate state diffeomorphism and input transformation have been found. The sufficient conditions use constant-rank involutive distributions and functions h1 and h2 supplied by Frobenius-style reasoning. The car example is useful because the abstract conditions become a concrete change of variables.

title: Optimal Steering Beyond Model Systems
notes: For a general driftless nonholonomic system, the closed-form sinusoid story becomes a necessary-condition story. The Hamiltonian calculation says the optimal controls equal minus the costate paired with each input vector field. Differentiating produces a skew-symmetric Omega matrix built from Lie brackets, so the control norm remains constant even when the actual time dependence is no longer a simple fixed-frequency sinusoid.

title: Philip Hall Coordinates
notes: Philip Hall coordinates are a way to make bracket bookkeeping finite and ordered for nilpotent systems. The Hall basis records only independent Lie words after skew-symmetry and Jacobi identities have been handled. In those coordinates every flow can be represented as a product of exponentials along Hall basis elements, while fictitious bracket inputs are introduced temporarily and later synthesized from real controls.

title: BCH Words Generate Brackets
notes: The Campbell-Baker-Hausdorff formula is the algebraic reason a word of flows can generate a bracket direction. The simple commutator loop cancels the first-order motion and leaves a second-order bracket term. Higher-order words work similarly, but nilpotency is the feature that keeps the expansion finite. Without nilpotency the same idea becomes an approximation scheme rather than an exact finite recipe.

title: Dynamic Finger Repositioning
notes: Return to manipulation by interpreting rolling contact as a nonholonomic planning problem. The grasp constraint relates finger velocities and object velocity. If there is a null space in the hand Jacobian, internal motions can move contacts while keeping the object fixed. This gives a clean reason to study a single rolling fingertip: the redundant degrees decouple when object motion is held at zero.

title: Geometric Phase From Rolling Loops
notes: The geometric-phase figure connects the chapter's area idea back to rolling contact. A closed path of the spherical fingertip can return the contact coordinates while changing the contact angle. The Gauss-Bonnet relation says that this phase is the negative area enclosed on the sphere. Stress that the accumulated phase is history-dependent; the loop is not wasted motion.

title: Constructive Controllability Checklist
notes: Close with the audit habit that the notebook encourages. A steering construction should declare its chart, identify the bracket or phase coordinate being targeted, use a loop or word whose lower-order terms cancel, and compare the endpoint with a scalar invariant. The linked final sanity and lab JSON files turn those claims into inspectable artifacts rather than purely verbal assurances.
